centrov: Old Town: Lipscani, Stavropoleos and Hanul lui Manuc

Bucharest's historic centre, a grid of 19th-century streets around Strada Lipscani, with restored buildings, restaurants and bars. Here are the small Stavropoleos Monastery, with its Brâncovenesc-style courtyard, the 1808 Hanul lui Manuc inn with its large inner courtyard and the ruins of the Curtea Veche, the palace of the princes of Wallachia.
parlament: The world's second-largest administrative building, ordered by the dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu in the 1980s: thousands of rooms, marble staircases and gigantic chandeliers. You visit in a group with a guide, in about an hour, through some of the halls.
ateneu: The Romanian Athenaeum is the city's concert hall, an 1888 neoclassical temple with a dome and a painted frieze of the country's history. Around it are Revolution Square, where Ceaușescu's regime fell in December 1989, the former Central Committee building and, on Calea Victoriei, the CEC Palace and the National Museum of Art.
carusel: A bookshop in a 1903 building, on six floors with white galleries, a high ceiling and light pouring in from above. On the top floor there's a bistro. One of the city's most photographed places, but you can buy a book or simply go up and look.
tarani: The Romanian peasant museum, one of the finest in Europe: costumes, icons painted on glass, textiles, traditional house interiors and a rebuilt wooden church. It's in a neo-Romanian building at the end of Calea Victoriei, near Piața Victoriei.
arcul: Bucharest's 27-metre triumphal arch, built in 1936 in honour of the Romanian army and the reunification. You can climb inside to the platform, with a view over Kiseleff Boulevard and the park.
satului: An open-air museum on the shore of Lake Herăstrău, with over 300 houses, wooden churches and mills brought from every region of Romania and arranged as villages. You walk among gardens, yards and workshops.
herastrau: The city's largest park, around a lake, with tree-lined avenues, a Japanese island, cycle paths and benches. It's where Bucharest residents go for a stroll, especially at weekends.
cismigiu: Bucharest's oldest public garden (1847), in the heart of the city, with a lake, flower beds, a writers' alley and outdoor tables. The most restful stop after the palaces of the centre.
cotroceni: The residence of the President of Romania, a historic palace partly open to the public as a museum: state rooms, apartments of the royal family and a small church. It's in the residential Cotroceni district, next to the botanical garden.
